title: Neck haematoma after thyroidectomy and hypocalcaemia

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care
guidelineVersions: DAS/BAETS/ENT-UK haematoma after thyroid surgery guideline (Sep 2021; Anaesthesia Jan 2022)
Society for Endocrinology acute hypocalcaemia guidance (Sep 2016; addendum Jun 2019)

brief.scenario: Mrs Anjali Raghavan, 46, had a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease this morning. Six hours later the nurse calls you: Mrs Raghavan's neck is swelling, it feels tight, and she is finding it hard to swallow. She looks anxious. RR 24, SpO2 94% on air, pulse 110.
brief.task: The examiner will ask how you would manage her. Later you will be asked about a problem the next morning.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: An expanding neck haematoma is an airway emergency: oxygen, help, and open the wound at the bedside. Then treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia with the exact IV regimen.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Leaving to phone for advice while her airway closes.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is a haematoma until proven otherwise. Oxygen, sit her up, and call for help now."

grid.label: Recognising the haematoma
grid.fail: Puts it down to anxiety or normal swelling and plans to review later.
grid.pass: Expanding haematoma threatening the airway: DESATS (difficulty swallowing, rising early warning score, swelling, anxiety, tachypnoea, stridor).
grid.high: Knows most occur within 24 hours, about half within 6; stridor can be late; a drain doesn't exclude it.

grid.label: Oxygen, position and help
grid.fail: Leaves the bedside to phone the registrar without giving oxygen.
grid.pass: Oxygen, head-up position, and help: senior surgeon, and a senior anaesthetist immediately because of airway signs.
grid.high: Brings the post-thyroid emergency box and front-of-neck kit, and alerts theatre early.

grid.label: Bedside evacuation: SCOOP (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Waits for theatre or the registrar while her airway worsens.
grid.pass: With airway compromise, opens the wound at the bedside: skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles, pack wound.
grid.high: Opens the strap muscles to release the deep clot; knows local anaesthetic isn't needed; then theatre for haemostasis.

grid.label: Airway if evacuation fails
grid.fail: Doesn't know what to do if she still can't breathe.
grid.pass: Anaesthetist intubates if compromise persists after evacuation; front-of-neck airway if cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate.
grid.high: Scalpel cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy rather than cannula; capnography confirms the tube; scalpel, bougie and 6.0 cuffed tube on the ward.

grid.label: Recognising hypocalcaemia
grid.pass: Perioral and finger paraesthesia, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, carpopedal spasm; can cause laryngospasm, seizures and a prolonged QT.
grid.high: Links it to parathyroid disruption at total thyroidectomy, the most frequent hospital cause; uses adjusted calcium.

grid.label: IV calcium (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Gives oral calcium alone, or pushes undiluted calcium fast without monitoring.
grid.borderline: Gives IV calcium gluconate but can't give the dilution, rate or monitoring.
grid.pass: Under 1.9 or symptomatic: 10–20 ml 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 ml 5% glucose IV over 10 minutes, with ECG monitoring.
grid.high: Repeats until symptoms settle, then infuses 100 ml 10% gluconate in 1 litre saline or 5% glucose at 50–100 ml/h, titrated.

grid.label: Cause and follow-on treatment
grid.fail: Doesn't check magnesium or plan beyond the bolus.
grid.pass: Checks magnesium, phosphate, PTH, U&E and vitamin D; starts alfacalcidol 0.25–0.5 micrograms daily for hypoparathyroidism.
grid.high: Knows calcium chloride is central-line only; mild asymptomatic cases get oral calcium and a repeat level at 24 hours.

grid.label: Communication afterwards
grid.fail: Doesn't explain what happened or document it.
grid.pass: Explains what happened, documents times and actions, and makes sure the consultant speaks with her.
grid.high: Offers referral for psychological support after an emergency evacuation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An expanding haematoma: she has difficulty swallowing, swelling, anxiety and tachypnoea. About half of these present within 6 hours. Stridor may come late, and a drain can clot and mislead.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Her swelling is growing and her voice is muffled.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: High-flow oxygen, head up. I'm staying: the nurse puts out a call for the senior anaesthetist and surgeon now. Bring the thyroid emergency box and front-of-neck kit, and alert theatre.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She now has stridor. The registrar is 10 minutes away.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I won't wait. SCOOP: expose the skin, cut the sutures, open the skin, open the strap muscles to release the deep clot, and pack. No local anaesthetic needed. Then theatre for haemostasis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If she's still obstructed, the anaesthetist intubates, ideally after evacuation. If they can't intubate or oxygenate, a scalpel cricothyroidotomy, not a cannula, confirmed with capnography.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Next morning she has tingling lips. Adjusted calcium 1.74.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia after total thyroidectomy, the most frequent cause in hospital. I'd look for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, and check the ECG for a long QT.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is an emergency: 10 to 20 ml of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 to 100 ml of 5% glucose over 10 minutes, with ECG monitoring, repeated until her symptoms settle. Then 100 ml of 10% gluconate in a litre of saline or 5% glucose at 50 to 100 ml an hour, titrated.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Magnesium, phosphate, PTH, U&E and vitamin D. Alfacalcidol 0.25 to 0.5 micrograms daily. Calcium chloride only through a central line.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She asks what happened last night.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd explain what happened and why, document the times, and make sure the consultant sees her, with an offer of psychological support.

failures.move: Waiting for the registrar or theatre while a patient with stridor deteriorates.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: complete airway obstruction and hypoxic arrest can follow within minutes.

failures.move: Leaving the bedside to make a phone call.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: she deteriorates unobserved, with no one ready to open the wound.

failures.move: Giving oral calcium alone to a symptomatic patient with adjusted calcium 1.74.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: this is a medical emergency; tetany, laryngospasm, seizures or arrhythmia can follow.

failures.move: Giving undiluted calcium chloride through a peripheral cannula.
failures.consequence: It irritates veins; the guidance restricts calcium chloride to a central line.

recovery.line: Whatever the letters, I open every layer of the wound at the bedside, including the muscles, and pack it.

recovery.when: You gave the calcium dose without dilution or rate
recovery.line: Let me be exact: diluted in 50 to 100 ml of 5% glucose, over 10 minutes, on ECG monitoring.

knowledge.fact: Haemorrhage after thyroid surgery: 0.45–4.2%; observations at least hourly for the first 6 hours.
Consider IV dexamethasone and tranexamic acid when there's concern but no immediate compromise.
Mild (asymptomatic, over 1.9): oral calcium; recheck at 24 hours; discharge above 2.1 with a check within 1 week.
Low magnesium: IV magnesium 24 mmol over 24 hours.
Each 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate contains 2.2 mmol of calcium.

recall.think: Airway obstruction; then tetany, laryngospasm and arrhythmia.
recall.say: "She has stridor: I'm opening the wound now."
do: Diluted IV calcium gluconate on ECG

numbers.meaning: 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 ml 5% glucose over 10 min
about half of haematomas present by then

recall.trap: A drain with little in it doesn't exclude a haematoma.
recall.finish: Theatre for haemostasis; calcium infusion titrated to normal, and alfacalcidol.

sources.supports: Haemorrhage incidence 0.45-4.2%; most within 24 hours, about half within 6 hours; observations at least hourly for 6 hours; DESATS (difficulty swallowing or discomfort, rise in EWS/NEWS, swelling, anxiety, tachypnoea or difficulty breathing, stridor); stridor may be a late sign; drains may give false reassurance; immediate oxygen and head-up position; immediate senior surgical review, and a senior anaesthetist immediately if airway compromise or no senior surgeon available; consider IV dexamethasone and tranexamic acid; with airway compromise open the wound at the bedside by SCOOP (skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles, pack wound), including the strap muscles; no local anaesthetic needed; alert theatre; intubate if compromise persists, attempting intubation after evacuation where compromise is imminent; capnography confirms tracheal intubation; scalpel cricothyroidotomy or emergency tracheostomy preferred to cannula in cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate; scalpel (number 10 blade), bougie and cuffed 6.0 mm tube on the ward; post-thyroid surgery emergency box at the bedside and on transfers; the consultant usually communicates with the patient afterwards, offering psychological support

sources.name: Turner J, Gittoes N, Selby P; Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee. Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypocalcaemia in adult patients. Endocr Connect 2016;5(5):G7-G8; with addendum, Endocr Connect 2019;8(6):X1
sources.supports: Symptoms typically below about 1.9 mmol/L adjusted calcium, depending on the rate of fall; features: perioral and digital paraesthesiae, Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs, tetany and carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, prolonged QT and arrhythmia, seizure; total thyroidectomy is the most common cause of acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia in hospital; investigations: adjusted calcium, phosphate, PTH, U&E, vitamin D, magnesium; mild (asymptomatic, over 1.9): oral calcium (e.g. Sandocal 1000 2 tablets twice daily); after thyroidectomy, recheck at 24 hours; discharge when adjusted calcium over 2.1 and recheck within 1 week; alfacalcidol 0.25 micrograms daily if still mildly low beyond 72 hours; hypomagnesaemia: IV magnesium 24 mmol over 24 hours; severe (under 1.9 and/or symptomatic at any level below the reference range) is a medical emergency: 10-20 ml 10% calcium gluconate in 50-100 ml 5% glucose IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring, repeated until asymptomatic, then 100 ml 10% calcium gluconate in 1 litre saline or 5% glucose at 50-100 ml/hour, titrated to normocalcaemia; calcium chloride only via a central line; alfacalcidol or calcitriol 0.25-0.5 micrograms daily for postoperative hypoparathyroidism; continuous ECG monitoring with arrhythmia or digoxin; each 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate contains 2.2 mmol calcium (addendum)

partner.opening: Mrs Raghavan's neck is swelling six hours after her thyroidectomy. What is going on, and what would you do?

reveals.trigger: Asks to examine the neck and see the observations
reveals.finding: Tense swelling across the front of the neck, larger over 20 minutes; voice muffled; no stridor yet. RR 24, SpO2 94% on air, pulse 110, BP 152/90. The drain holds 10 ml.
RR 30, soft inspiratory stridor, SpO2 90% on 15 L oxygen. The registrar is 10 minutes away; the anaesthetist is on the way.
Dark clot is released; her breathing eases and SpO2 rises to 97%. Theatre can take her in 15 minutes.

reveals.trigger: Moving on to the next morning
reveals.finding: Day 1, 08:00: tingling around her lips and fingers. Chvostek's sign positive. Adjusted calcium 1.74 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 490 ms.
Magnesium 0.82, phosphate 1.52, PTH low, potassium 4.1. Not on digoxin.

push.question: What do the letters of SCOOP stand for?
push.expect: Skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles, pack wound.

push.question: How exactly would you give the calcium, and what then?
push.expect: 10–20 ml 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 ml 5% glucose over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring; repeat until asymptomatic; then an infusion of 100 ml 10% in 1 L at 50–100 ml/h, titrated.

push.question: Why is her calcium low?
push.expect: Disruption of parathyroid function at total thyroidectomy (hypoparathyroidism): low PTH.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Correct it: IV magnesium 24 mmol over 24 hours, and monitor the level.

curveballs.prompt: The only calcium on the ward is 10 ml of 10% calcium chloride.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Calcium chloride is more irritant and should go through a central line; get calcium gluconate or senior advice.

curveballs.prompt: A nurse asks for lidocaine before you open the wound.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Local anaesthetic isn't needed; don't delay opening the wound.
